store.0: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite challenging, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to for a while. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even exploring the basics of quantum computing. It's a thrilling experience!

store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by theory that directly connects to real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. We've been exploring dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending at times. However, our professor is excellent at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a seemingly impossible problem and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with ideas and insights.
store.3: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, my second most challenging class this semester is Distributed Systems(CS 2631). It's a lot of reading and group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with individuals who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about the final product. However, that's also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues such as concurrency and node failures gracefully. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.4: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. The professor is from the industry and has worked on a couple of indie games that received decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even exploring user experience design. The assignments are incredibly creative, and I find it unbelievably fun. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on balancing the difficulty curve to prevent players from getting frustrated and quitting. It was challenging to get the design right, but it was rewarding to see it come together.
store.5: I initially thought I might regret signing up for the Introduction to Quantum Computing class, but now I actually enjoy it. The professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math, which makes it more accessible. Of course, there is still math involved, such as linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff that has made me rethink how I approach problems.
store.6: The Capstone Project course is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.7: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding in my other classes. It's nice to sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was a fascinating experience. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.8: My typical college schedule is quite packed. Mondays and Wednesdays are the most hectic days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are slightly lighter with just Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. On Thursdays, I also have Philosophy of Mind in the evening, which can be tough if I'm already tired from the day. Fridays are usually free of scheduled classes, but I always end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also make time for undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's fascinating, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm just trying to make the most of my senior year and push through the challenges.
store.9: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and it can be even more time-consuming if we encounter a major bug or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating the schedules of five different people can be a mini-nightmare, but despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of an actual job environment. It's a great opportunity to apply everything I've learned and push myself to the limit.
store.10: Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's never as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.
store.11: I'm a fourth-year computer science major, and my hobbies are what keep me sane amidst a hectic schedule of classes and projects. I find that my outside interests help me approach programming with a fresh perspective. It's essential to take breaks and not be stuck behind my laptop 24/7, even if I enjoy coding.

store.13: Sailing is a unique hobby that brings me a sense of freedom and challenge. I grew up near a marina and started sailing with my dad on small sailboats. The rush of wind against the sails hooked me from the beginning. Now in college, I try to keep up with sailing during breaks by renting a boat from a local sailing club. It's a great way to escape the stress of deadlines, code bugs, and group project drama. Sailing requires problem-solving on a grand scale, which appeals to my nerdy side. I love the unpredictable nature of the water and wind, making each experience a thrilling puzzle to solve.

store.15: Regular gym visits are a significant part of my routine. I started with a basic lifting routine in college, thanks to a friend who taught me proper form and programming techniques. Now, I aim to go to the gym around four times a week. It's not about becoming a bodybuilder, but I enjoy seeing incremental improvements in my strength and energy levels. Working out helps me relieve stress after long coding sessions and enhances my mental clarity, making me more productive and helping me sleep better. It's a vital part of my self-care routine.

store.17: Gaming is another hobby that complements my interest in technology. I enjoy both PC and console games, but PC gaming is more convenient for me as a CS major. Lately, I've been fascinated by co-op survival games where I can gather resources, build shelters, and fend off creatures. This genre offers a more relaxed problem-solving experience compared to debugging code. I also occasionally join fast-paced shooters when friends from class are online, which adds a social and mental challenge to my gaming routine. I believe gaming can be strategic and collaborative, allowing me to stay connected with others. Additionally, I've experimented with game development using Unity and Unreal Engine, and I hope to delve deeper into it if time allows. Bridging the gap between playing games and creating them is truly exciting.

store.19: Reading has been a lifelong passion for me, thanks to my mom's love for literature. She introduced me to fantasy and sci-fi novels when I was a kid, and I'd get lost in other worlds for hours. Even with a busy schedule, I try to squeeze in some reading before bed or on weekends. Lately, I've been fascinated by sci-fi novels that explore artificial intelligence. It's a combination of my academic interests and curiosity about future technology and its impact on humanity. My current favorite AI-themed sci-fi book is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. Reading books like this helps me consider the ethical and social implications of the work I'll be doing after graduation, making it more than just a relaxation activity.

store.21: Scheduling my hobbies is crucial in maintaining a healthy balance. I plan my week ahead, checking the weather to determine if I can fit in outdoor activities like gym visits or sailing trips. If the weather isn't cooperating, I'll plan indoor activities like co-op gaming or working out in my apartment's fitness center. Reading is the easiest to fit in, and I make sure to set aside 30 minutes before bedtime to unwind. By being intentional with my time, I'm able to enjoy my hobbies while also managing my academic responsibilities.

It's great to see how different activities can complement each other in such meaningful ways.

store.25: I understand that life can be stressful, especially with a heavy academic workload. However, when you're passionate about your hobbies, you'll find ways to fit them into your schedule, even if it's just in small increments. For example, I might not have time for hours of reading, but I can squeeze in one chapter. Similarly, I might not be able to sail every weekend, but once a month works. And even with a busy schedule, I can fit in a quick gaming match if I have 30 minutes to spare. It's all about being intentional with your time and finding ways to make your hobbies a part of your daily life.
